name: overhead-from-the-top
prompt: Every gang member wears a knitted balaclava covering the whole head, with no eye, nose or mouth holes; a large white ring is stitched round the face, and a red triangle sits high over the wearer's left eye (on the right of the picture, at about 2 o'clock); gloves on both hands, collars and cuffs closed, no skin showing anywhere. Portrait-format night shot, camera pointing ninety degrees downward from the summit of a towering block of paper reams in a disused warehouse: a vertical cliff of white page edges plunges away beneath us, narrowing hard as it drops towards a rain-slicked concrete slab a long way down. Filling the near foreground, almost touching the lens, is the topmost sheet, its paper grain crisp, bearing two words set in a fat bold black sans-serif: THE RULES. At the very foot of that paper cliff, small, foreshortened and gently blurred, a cluster of four masked figures in ordinary present-day British clothes (a parka, a zipped tracksuit top, a work fleece, a rain jacket, scuffed trainers) crane their necks back so their faces point up at us; each mask is knitted in its own dark tone, one forest green, one ink blue, one maroon, one slate. Three of them aim pocket torches skyward, so thin white shafts rise up the page edges and make the white ring and red triangle on each mask gleam against the dark wool. The one other source is a dim sodium-orange glow falling through a dirty skylight-height window onto a puddle beside them, where the torch beams also shimmer. Everything outside those pools of light sinks to pure black; ultra-wide lens, extreme converging verticals, deep drop between foreground page and floor, sharp focus on the type, soft focus on the figures, subtle grain, no haze. The sense is reversed vertigo: the paper itself towering over them and staring down.
